ety.text: From Middle English killen, kyllen, cüllen (“to strike, beat, cut”), of obscure origin. Cognate with Scots kele, keil (“to kill”). * Perhaps from unattested Old English *cyllan, from Proto-West Germanic *kwulljan, from Proto-Germanic *kwuljaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷelH- (“to throw, hit, hurt by throwing”). * Or, possibly a variant of Old English cwellan (“to kill, murder, execute”) (see quell). * Or, from Old Norse kolla (“to hit on the head, harm”), related to Norwegian kylla (“to poll”), Middle Dutch kollen (“to knock down”), Icelandic kollur (“top, head”); see also coll, cole).

ety.text: Proto-Indo-European *ǵeyH-der. Proto-Indo-European *ǵi(H)-l-der. Proto-Germanic *kiljǭ Proto-West Germanic *killjā Old Dutch *killa Middle Dutch kille Dutch kilbor. English kill Borrowing from Dutch kil (formerly spelled kill), from Middle Dutch kille, from Old Dutch *killa, from Proto-West Germanic *killjā, from Proto-Germanic *kiljǭ (“fissure, slit; a type of stream, creek, channel”). Doublet of Kiel.

senses.d: To put to death; to extinguish the life of.
ex: Smoking kills more people each year than alcohol and hard drugs combined.
As the country reckons with how to prevent more children from being killed at school, the legacies of the Parkland victims live on.

senses.d: To render inoperative.
ex: He killed the engine and turned off the headlights, but remained in the car, waiting.
He killed the motor.

senses.d: To stop, cease, or render void; to terminate.
ex: The editor decided to kill the story.
The news that a hurricane had destroyed our beach house killed our plans to sell it.

senses.d: To amaze, exceed, stun, or otherwise incapacitate.
ex: That night, she was dressed to kill.
That joke always kills me.

senses.d: To cause great pain, discomfort, or distress to; to hurt.
ex: These tight shoes are killing my feet.
You don't ever want to get rabies. The doctor will have to give you multiple shots and they really kill.

senses.d: To produce feelings of dissatisfaction or revulsion in.
ex: It kills me to throw out three whole turkeys, but I can't get anyone to take them and they've already started to go bad.
It kills me to learn how many poor people are practically starving in this country while rich moguls spend such outrageous amounts on useless luxuries.

senses.d: To use up or to waste.
ex: I'm just doing this to kill time.

senses.d: To overpower, overwhelm, or defeat.
ex: Look at the amount of destruction to the enemy base. We pretty much killed their ability to retaliate.
The team had absolutely killed their traditional rivals, and the local sports bars were raucous with celebrations.

senses.d: To force a company out of business.
To punish severely.
ex: My parents are going to kill me!
"Father will kill us for this."

senses.d: The act of killing.
ex: The assassin liked to make a clean kill, and thus favored small arms over explosives.

senses.d: Specifically, the death blow.
ex: The hunter delivered the kill with a pistol shot to the head.

senses.d: The result of killing; that which has been killed.
ex: The fox dragged its kill back to its den.
If ye plunder his kill from a weaker, devour not all in thy pride.

senses.d: An instance of killing; a score on the tally of enemy personnel or vehicles killed or destroyed.
ex: confirmed kills
A flying ace is usually one with five or more confirmed kills.

senses.d: The grounding of the ball on the opponent's court, winning the rally.
A creek or stream; (more loosely) any watercourse, such as a channel or arm of the sea.
ex: The channel beyond Staten Island, which connects Newark Bay with Bergen Neck is the Kill van Kull, or the Kills.

senses.d: In particular, a waterway with a name ending in kill, such as the Beaverkill or the East Kill.
ex: We're gonna go flyfishing over in the kill.

senses.d: One who or that which kills.
ex: There’s a killer on the loose.
My cat is a habitual bird killer.

senses.d: That which causes stress or is extremely difficult, especially that which may cause failure at a task.
ex: That test was a killer.
The final hill in the race course was a killer.

senses.d: Something that is so far ahead of its competition that it effectively kills off that competition.
ex: Digital streaming platforms are CD killers.

senses.d: The killer whale.
ex: Fig. 188.—Grampus or Killer, Orca gladiator. (Flower, art. “Mammalia,” ‘Encyclopædia Britannica.’)
We once saw an attack made by three killers upon a cow whale and her calf, in a lagoon on the coast of California in the spring of 1858.

senses.d: A remarkably impressive person or thing.
ex: Picture perfect, you don't need no filter / Gorgeous, make 'em drop dead, you're a killer

senses.d: A knockout form of darts or pool involving several players.
A club used for killing fish.

Excellent, very good, cool.

killer view

senses.d: Causing death, destruction, or obliteration.
ex: killer bee
killer robot

senses.d: Distressing, uncomfortable.
ex: I had a killer headache this morning.

senses.d: That makes one ‘die’ with laughter; very funny.

senses.d: The act of killing.

senses.d: An instance of someone being killed.
ex: The outrage over the brutal killings of peaceful demonstrators in Lhasa in March 1989 quickly faded after the massacres in Beijing in June.

senses.d: A large amount of money.
ex: He made a killing on the stock market.
